For me, even though I was born and raised in a southern state, I've never had strong feelings one way or the other regarding that flag - it was just something people put on trucks and t-shirts and over the windows of their trailer because of where they were from. But I also understand that it can only be that 'generic symbol of the south' when separated from it's historical context. Personally, I think it's obvious from historical documents that the prime catalyst for the Civil War was slavery, but even if you disagree, there's plenty of evidence that white supremacy was a big deal to the founding fathers of the confederacy. Alexander Stephens, VP of the confederate states said he disagreed with the Declaration of Independence because all men weren't created equal:

“Our new Government is founded upon exactly the opposite idea; its foundations are laid, its cornerstone rests, upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery, subordination to the superior race, is his natural and normal condition.”

So I've never really understood the 'heritage' argument, because why is that a heritage you want to associate yourself with? White supremacists that lost a war - yeah, that sounds like the team I want to be on. /s

But even if I don't really care one way or the other for the flag itself, I feel like it's an important distinction to make that the confederate flag hasn't been banned.

Any individual in America is still free to buy, sell, trade, or display the confederate flag (or rather, the battle flag popularly referred to as the confederate flag). The reason it's an important distinction to me is because if the flag had been banned, I would suddenly care very much about the issue.

As it stands, though, in the simplest terms, what's happened is some private corporations have made a decision about what they do and don't want to sell to the public - being opposed to that is standing against capitalism - and a state government has made a decision based on their constituents' opinions about what's appropriate for their state building - that's democracy at work. In both cases, I feel like these are positive things.

The classic illustration of 'dangerous speech' is falsely yelling 'fire' in a crowded theater. The first danger is to life and limb, of course, but you also risk the theater itself - being "that place where people get trampled all the time because idiots keep yelling 'fire'" isn't great for business. So, if you enjoy the services the theater provides you, it's foolish to make decisions that ultimately harm it.

America is the theater, the confederate flag is yelling 'fire'. Whatever someone's personal reasons for supporting that flag, it's worth acknowledging that large segments of our population feel differently towards it, and with good reason, and that there is a deepening societal rift that is only being made worse by those insisting on exercising their right to fly it. That's what Wal-Mart saw. That's what Amazon saw. That's what the leadership of South Carolina saw. It's not so much "this might hurt someone's feelings" or "this has a checkered past", it's "a nation divided cannot stand". It's that if we truly love the freedoms that America gives us, it's our responsibility to not use them in ways that weaken our unity as a nation. I just don't think the stars and stripes has the same divisive power as the stars and bars, and that's what makes it a different situation than the American flag to Native Americans.

The flip side of that coin being that the 'fire in a crowded theater' argument was initially used in an appeal to get the supreme court to silence those opposed to the US instituting the draft during WWI. I don't want to live under a government that would ban the confederate flag, because allowing a government to label symbols 'dangerous' and silence those that disagree doesn't lead to a country I want to live in. But I'll be happy - nay, proud - to live in a country that didn't have to do that, because it's citizens exercised their own personal responsibility without requiring government intervention.
